title: Coat Drive Handout
story: A winter coat drive has a pile of donated coats, each tagged with a warmth rating. Each person in line tells you the lowest rating that will keep them warm, and is happy with any coat rated at least that.
Each coat goes to one person, and each person takes at most one coat. Get as many people as possible walking away warm.
task: Write maxWarmPeople(needs, coats). needs[i] is the lowest warmth person i accepts. coats[j] is the warmth of coat j. Return the largest number of people who can each get a coat with coats[j] ≥ needs[i].
Either list may be empty; then the answer is 0. Neither list is sorted.

examples.explanation: The coat rated 2 is too thin for everyone. The 4 can go to the person needing 3, and the 5 can go to the person needing 4. No coat is warm enough for the person needing 6, so 2 people get coats.
If you hand out the first coat that fits, the person needing 2 takes the 8 and the person needing 7 gets nothing. If you give the 2 to the first person and the 8 to the second, both are warm.

hints: In the second example, the person who needs 2 could take either coat. Which should they take so you lose as little as possible?
A coat warmer than needed wastes warmth. Serve each person with the thinnest coat that works, and save warm coats for people who need them.
Sort both lists. If the thinnest coat is not warm enough for the least needy person, can it be warm enough for anyone?

Sort needs and coats. Walk the coats from thinnest to warmest with a pointer into the sorted needs. If the coat covers the current least needy person, they are served and the pointer moves on; otherwise skip the coat. The pointer's final position is the answer.
bruteForce: Try every way of handing out coats: for each person, each unused coat that fits, or none, and keep the best total. The number of matchings explodes: even 20 people and 20 coats is far beyond any computer.

A gentler first idea gives each person in line the first coat in the pile that fits. It is fast but wrong: in the second example a needy person loses out because a warm coat went to someone who needed very little.

js: * @param {number[]} needs  lowest warmth each person accepts
* @return {number} most people who can get a coat
py: def max_warm_people(needs: list[int], coats: list[int]) -> int:

js: let served = 0; // index of the least needy person still waiting
served++; // thinnest coat that works goes to this person
// otherwise this coat is too thin for everyone left: skip it
py: served = 0  # index of the least needy person still waiting
if served < len(people) and coat >= people[served]:
served += 1  # thinnest coat that works goes to this person
# otherwise this coat is too thin for everyone left: skip it
walkthrough: The greedy rule: starting from the thinnest coat, give each coat to the least needy person it can serve. A thin coat has the fewest possible owners, so spend it on the easiest person to please and keep warm coats free.
Trace the first example. Sorted needs: [3, 4, 6]. Sorted coats: [2, 4, 5].
• Coat 2: the least needy person wants 3, and 2 is less than 3, so this coat fits nobody and is skipped.
• Coat 4: the least needy person still waiting wants 3, and 4 is at least 3, so that person takes it. One person is served.
• Coat 5: the next person wants 4, and 5 is at least 4, so that person takes it. Two people are served.
• There are no coats left, so the person needing 6 goes without. The answer is 2.
Skipping a coat is safe: if it cannot cover the least needy person left, it cannot cover anyone, since everyone else needs at least as much.
solution.time: O(n log n + m log m)
solution.timeWhy: Sorting both lists dominates. The matching itself is one pass over the coats.
solution.spaceWhy: The two sorted copies take this space. Sorting the input lists in place would reduce it to the memory the sort itself uses.
solution.takeaway: To match items to requests that each have a minimum, sort both sides and pair the smallest request with the smallest item that works. Spending the least valuable resource that does the job keeps the valuable ones free.
